const cmd = `cat > '/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s001/discovery/pilot1-20261005/1_4/luna/list.tsv' <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Deut.32.36	דין / yādîn	The Hebrew verb yādîn, “he will judge,” is cognate with the commentary’s labeled Arabic d-y-n; here YHWH judges his people and vindicates them against their oppressors.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Dan.7.10	Aramaic dînâ	The Aramaic court term dînâ is cognate with Arabic dīn; in the same verse the court sits and books are opened, so the cognate occurs in a concrete judgment scene.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Isa.33.22	מֶלֶךְ / melekh	Hebrew melekh, “king,” is cognate with the commentary’s labeled Arabic m-l-k; Isaiah uses it for the Lord beside “judge” and “lawgiver.”
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.74.17	יוֹם / yôm	Hebrew yôm is cognate with the commentary’s labeled Arabic y-w-m; this verse says day and night belong to God and names the appointed light and sun.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.33.22	Judge, lawgiver, king, savior	The commentary lets mālik carry both possession and rule; Isaiah places the Lord’s judicial, legislative, royal, and saving roles in one verse.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Chr.29.11	All things and kingship belong to God	David’s prayer assigns everything in heaven and earth, and the kingdom itself, to God; this makes human ownership provisional beside the Day’s sole owner.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.18.25	Judge of all the earth	Abraham asks whether the judge of all the earth will do what is just; the universal jurisdiction gives the commentary’s judgment day a concrete biblical counterpart.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.32.35	Divine repayment	Within Moses’ song, God reserves vengeance and repayment for the appointed time; this links the day’s closing account with a reckoning that no human claimant controls.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.24.16	No one answers for another	The law says parents and children die for their own offenses, not one another’s; it parallels the commentary’s day when no person can own or pay another’s account.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Eccl.12.14	Every deed, including the hidden	At the close of Ecclesiastes, God brings every deed to judgment, even what is concealed; this matches the commentary’s expansion from public evidence to inward acts.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.34.11	Repayment according to deeds	Elihu says God repays a person according to what that person has done; the direct correspondence is the commentary’s account settled in full on the owned day.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.17.10	Heart searched and ways repaid	The Lord searches the heart and gives each person according to conduct; this connects the commentary’s private intention and heart-accounting with an explicit biblical judgment formula.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Sam.2.3	Deeds weighed	Hannah says the Lord weighs actions; this gives the commentary’s image of an unbending scale a moral use, not merely a lexical association with measure.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.16.11	Just scales belong to the Lord	Proverbs says honest balances and weights are the Lord’s; the commentary likewise makes the final account a measure whose standard belongs to the day’s owner.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Dan.5.27	Weighed and found wanting	Daniel interprets the king’s writing as a verdict that he was weighed and found deficient; it turns the commentary’s balance image into a royal judgment scene.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Dan.7.10	Court and opened books	Daniel sees the court seated and books opened before the Ancient of Days; this closely matches the commentary’s tribunal, record, witnesses, and full payment of deeds.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mal.3.16	Book of remembrance	Malachi records the words of those who fear the Lord in a book before him; the written record parallels the commentary’s books that preserve what people did.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.49.8	Ransom cannot rescue a brother	WLC numbering includes the psalm heading; in English numbering this is Psalm 49:7. The singer says no person can ransom a brother from death, matching the day when no one can pay another’s due.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.1.21	Wealth left behind	Job says he came naked from the womb and will return naked; this sharpens the commentary’s image of property and servants left behind when a person comes alone.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Dan.12.2	The dead awake to opposed destinies	Daniel describes sleepers in the dust awakening to everlasting life or disgrace; it supplies resurrection and final outcome for the commentary’s day of reckoning.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Zeph.1.14	The great day arrives	Zephaniah calls the Lord’s day near and bitter, a day of battle cries; the day is an approaching event that overtakes people, as the commentary emphasizes.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.34.4	Heavens rolled like a scroll	Isaiah pictures the heavens rolled up like a scroll as the host falls; this matches the commentary’s cosmic unmaking, in which the sky can no longer serve as a clock.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Joel.2.10	Sun and moon darkened	Joel’s day of the Lord darkens the sun and moon and shakes the heavens; the signs make the commentary’s judgment day exceed ordinary solar measurement.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Amos.8.9	Sun sets at noon	Amos announces darkness at midday as judgment on Israel; unlike the final day in the commentary, this is a historical oracle, but it makes the solar clock fail at the moment of reckoning.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.90.5	A thousand years before God	WLC numbering includes the psalm heading; this is English Psalm 90:4. A thousand years are like yesterday before God, matching the commentary’s day whose measure is not the sun’s daily course.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Hab.2.3	Appointed time that surely comes	The vision waits for its appointed time and will not fail to arrive; this connects the commentary’s “falling/coming event” sense of the day with an event whose date is delayed but certain.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mic.7.4	Day of visitation	The prophet says the day of the watchmen and punishment has come amid social collapse; Micah’s next verses name betrayal within households, echoing the commentary’s day when ties fail.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mic.7.6	Household ties break down	Son, daughter, and daughter-in-law turn against close kin; in Micah this follows the announced day of punishment, a concrete social image for the commentary’s fleeing family bonds.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Zech.7.9	Justice joined to compassion	Zechariah commands true justice and mercy, then forbids oppressing widow, orphan, stranger, and poor; this joins the commentary’s judgment day to its contrast between mercy and punishment.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.74.17	God owns day and night	The same verse also works as a motif: day, night, sun, and light are under God’s ordering, making time itself part of the sovereignty the commentary assigns to the Day.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.10.18	Judge who feeds and clothes the vulnerable	God executes justice for orphan and widow and gives food and clothing to the stranger; this connects the commentary’s merciful owner with concrete care for those who lack worldly power.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 35:14-17	Impartial judge hears the poor	Sirach says God judges without favoritism and hears the wronged, orphan, and widow; this puts mercy toward the vulnerable inside the same final-account framework as the commentary.
strong	tevrat	motif	Wisdom of Solomon 11:23-26	All are God’s and spared by mercy	Wisdom says God loves what exists and spares it because it is his; this joins the commentary’s ownership language to the mercy that precedes its judgment title.
strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Genesis Rabbah 12:15	Mercy placed before strict judgment	The midrash says creation could not stand by strict justice alone, so mercy was placed first and justice joined to it; this illuminates Fatiha’s sequence of Rahman/Rahim before the Day of judgment.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 3:1	Account before the Creator	Akavya tells each person to consider where they came from, where they go, and before whom they will give account; it gives the commentary’s solitary arrival a Jewish ethical formulation.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 3:16	Open ledger and daily collectors	The shopkeeper gives credit, the ledger is open, and collectors regularly collect; the image makes the commentary’s debt, record, due date, and final repayment unusually concrete.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 4:22	Judgment before the King of Kings	The saying pairs unavoidable death with judgment before the King of Kings, matching the commentary’s sovereign who owns the day and the account due then.
strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Rosh Hashanah 16b	Books opened for judgment	The Talmud pictures three books opened on Rosh Hashanah for the righteous, wicked, and intermediate; it develops the commentary’s book-and-verdict image into a graded inscription tradition.
strong	tevrat	motif	Shabbat 31a	Conduct examined after death	The Talmud’s questions at judgment include whether one dealt faithfully in business and pursued wisdom; this makes ordinary habits part of the account, as the commentary says sustained conduct is judged.
strong	tevrat	paralel	1 Enoch 47:3	Throne and books of the living	Enoch sees the Head of Days on his throne as the books of the living are opened; this is a close Jewish apocalyptic court scene for the commentary’s records and final accounting.
strong	tevrat	paralel	4 Ezra 7:33-35	Judgment remains when patience ends	At the world’s end the Most High appears on the judgment seat and recompense follows; this parallels the commentary’s day when the account is complete and no earthly claim can alter it.
strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Avinu Malkeinu, Rosh Hashanah liturgy	King and book of life	The prayer addresses God as “Our Father, our King” and asks for inscription in the book of life; it holds royal sovereignty and hoped-for mercy together in a judgment-season setting.
strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Matt.25.31	The Son of Man enthroned as King	Jesus’ discourse places the glorious Son of Man on a throne before the nations are judged; it gives the commentary’s “owner of the day” a concrete royal court scene.
strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Matt.25.32	Shepherd separates the gathered peoples	The king separates people as a shepherd sorts sheep from goats; this joins the commentary’s day of division to its image of a leader whose destination determines the followers’ fate.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.35	Water given to the thirsty	At judgment, giving drink to a thirsty person is evidence of mercy; the commentary instead shows condemned people asking for water and being refused, so the shared water scene exposes opposite outcomes.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.24	Afterlife plea for water	The rich man asks Abraham to send Lazarus with water for his burning tongue; this closely matches the commentary’s damned who call across the divide for water.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.26	A fixed gulf blocks aid	Abraham says a great chasm prevents passage between the two sides; it explains why the water plea in Luke cannot be met and parallels the commentary’s closed access to the saved community’s water.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.18.27	A master cancels a debt	The king has compassion and releases a servant by cancelling his enormous debt; this is a specific Christian image for the commentary’s owner who can forgive what is owed on the day of settlement.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.16.27	Each repaid according to deeds	The Son of Man comes in glory and repays each person according to conduct; it directly matches the commentary’s account fully paid to every person.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.2.16	Secrets judged through Christ	Paul says God judges people’s secrets through Christ; this is a precise bridge to the commentary’s claim that hidden intentions enter the final account.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.5.10	Everyone before the judgment seat	Paul says all must appear before Christ’s judgment seat to receive for what was done in the body; it joins individual embodiment and deeds to the commentary’s personal reckoning.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.4.13	Nothing hidden from the judge	The author says no creature is concealed and all are exposed before the one to whom account must be given; this matches the commentary’s turn from public records to the heart’s hidden contents.
strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Rev.20.12	Books opened and the dead judged	John sees the dead judged by what is written in opened books, each according to deeds; this is a close Christian counterpart to the commentary’s court, records, and full recompense.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.19.1	Praise after true judgments	After Babylon’s fall, the heavenly crowd praises God because his judgments are true and just; this parallels the commentary’s praise formula voiced after judgment is completed.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.6.12	Sun and moon lose their light	The sun turns dark and the moon like blood as the day of wrath unfolds; this matches the commentary’s judgment scene in which the sun ceases to measure the day.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.6.14	Sky rolls up like a scroll	John sees the sky vanish like a rolled scroll; this is a close image for the commentary’s cosmic collapse and the end of ordinary celestial order.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Pet.3.8	A day unlike ordinary duration	Peter compares a day before the Lord to a thousand years; this makes explicit the commentary’s contrast between solar days and divine time.
strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Acts.17.31	An appointed day and righteous judgment	Paul says God fixed a day to judge the world in righteousness, with resurrection as assurance; the verse directly links day, divine judgment, and resurrection.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.2.13	Mercy at judgment	James says judgment is without mercy for one who has shown no mercy, while mercy triumphs over judgment; this holds the commentary’s mercy and wrath together as an ethical test.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:John.5.22	Judgment assigned to the Son	John says the Father has entrusted all judgment to the Son; this differs from the commentary’s emphasis on God as sole owner and final judge by assigning the court’s execution to a distinct divine figure.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.8.34	Christ intercedes at God’s right hand	Paul identifies the risen Christ as intercessor; beside the commentary’s speech and intercession available only by the Rahman’s leave, this gives that permitted role a specific Christian mediator.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.15	Only Sovereign, King of kings	The doxology calls God the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords; it complements the commentary’s distinction between possession and rule by declaring ultimate royal authority.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.20	Stored wealth cannot accompany the dead	God tells the rich fool that his life is demanded that night and asks who will own his stores; this dramatizes the commentary’s claim that worldly property stays behind when a person comes alone.
strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:1Cor.15.52	Last trumpet and resurrection	Paul says the trumpet sounds and the dead are raised imperishable; this supplies the resurrection event behind the commentary’s final-day accounting.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.9.27	Death followed by judgment	The author links death once with judgment afterward; this brings the commentary’s deathbed scene and the day of account into one sequence.
strong	incil	yorum_gelenegi	Augustine, City of God 20.1	Patristic reading of the last judgment	Augustine’s discussion of the final judgment around Revelation 20 treats it as a public reckoning of the dead; it gives the commentary’s opened court and day-as-event a major Christian interpretive frame.
strong	incil	yorum_gelenegi	John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew 78	The King’s judgment measured by mercy	Chrysostom’s homily on Matthew 25 reads feeding and giving drink to the needy as the King’s criterion at judgment; it clarifies the ethical weight of the commentary’s denied water and neglected poor.
strong	incil	motif	Dies Irae, stanzas 2-5	Judge, trumpet, and opened book	The hymn imagines the judge arriving, the trumpet summoning the dead, and a written record disclosing deeds; it gathers the commentary’s day, resurrection, and account into Christian liturgical language.
EOF`;
const r = await tools.exec_command({cmd, workdir: "/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation", max_output_tokens: 2000});
text(r.output || `wrote file (exit ${r.exit_code})`);

## Övgünün bir güne uzanması

Dördüncü ayet tek başına bir cümle değildir. İkinci ayet {ar:ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ, tr:el-hamdü lillâh, gloss:hamd Allah'adır, source:1:2} diye başlar ve Allah'ı art arda gelen adlarla anlatır: âlemlerin Rabbi, Rahman, Rahim ve şimdi {ar:مَٰلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ, tr:mâliki yevmi'd-dîn, gloss:din gününün sahibi, source:1:4}. "Mâliki" kelimesinin sonundaki esre onu bu zincire bağlar. Hamd hâlâ sürmektedir. Önceki adlar varlıkların bütününe ve rahmete uzanıyordu. Bu ad ise bir zamana uzanır. İnsan bir toprağa, bir sürüye ya da bir eve sahip olur, burada sahip olunan şey ise bir gündür. Bir zamanın sahibi olmak, o zamanda olacak her şeyin onun elinde olması demektir. Sahibin adı anıldıktan sonra konuşma yüz yüze döner.

<!-- v16:augment brief=augment9 model=opus para=1 kind=prose ref=39:75 -->

Fâtiha'nın ikinci ayetindeki söz, aynı kelimelerle, hükmün verildiği günün son cümlesi olarak duyulur. Fiil edilgendir ve sözü kimin söylediği bildirilmez. Aynı ayette melekler Arş'ın çevresini kuşatmış, Rablerini hamd ile tesbih ederken görülür.

<!-- v16:augment brief=augment9 model=opus para=1 kind=refs -->
Ayrıca: {source:28:70} hamdin hem ilk hayatta hem âhirette O'na ait olması ve hükmün O'nun olması; {source:34:1} âhiretteki hamdin de O'na ait olması; {source:10:10} cennettekilerin son sözünün "el-hamdü lillâhi rabbi'l-âlemîn" olması; {source:83:6} insanların âlemlerin Rabbi için ayağa kalktığı gün; {source:3:27} {source:6:13} zamanın sahipliği: geceyi gündüze katması, gecede ve gündüzde barınan her şeyin O'nun olması

Kelimenin yazısında mim harfinin üstündeki küçük elif uzun "â" sesini gösterir. Harflerin gövdesi m-l-k'dir. Kur'an Allah'ı bu kökten iki ayrı kelimeyle anar. Peygambere şöyle dua etmesi söylenir: {ar:قُلِ ٱللَّهُمَّ مَٰلِكَ ٱلْمُلْكِ, tr:kulillâhümme mâlike'l-mülk, gloss:de ki: Allah'ım, ey mülkün sahibi, source:3:26}. Kur'an'ın son suresinde ise sığınılan, "insanların Rabbi"dir ve hemen ardından O, {ar:مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ, tr:meliki'n-nâs, gloss:insanların hükümdarı, source:114:2} ve {ar:إِلَٰهِ ٱلنَّاسِ, tr:ilâhi'n-nâs, gloss:insanların ilahı, source:114:3} diye anılır. Rab, hükümdar ve ilah sırası Fâtiha'daki Allah, Rab ve sahip sırasıyla aynı malzemeden kurulur. "Mâlik" (sahip) ile "melik" (hükümdar) aynı kökten iki ayrı kelimedir. Araplar ikisini Allah için yan yana da söylerdi: {ar:الملك لله المالك المليك, tr:el-mülkü lillâhi'l-mâliki'l-melîk, gloss:mülk, sahip ve hükümdar olan Allah'ındır, source:"م ل ك,B003"}. Sahip elinde tuttuğunu kullanır. Hükümdar ise bir topluluğu yönetir: {ar:الملك هو المتصرف بالأمر والنهي في الجمهور, tr:el-melikü hüve'l-mütesarrifü bi'l-emri ve'n-nehyi fi'l-cumhûr, gloss:melik, topluluk üzerinde emir ve yasakla tasarruf edendir, source:"م ل ك,B003"}. Türkçede "memleket" bugün insanın doğup büyüdüğü yer ya da bir ülke demektir. Arapçada ise kelime toprağı değil, bir yetkiyi adlandırır: {ar:المملكة سلطان الملك في رعيته, tr:el-memleketü sultânü'l-meliki fî raiyyetih, gloss:memleket, hükümdarın halkı üzerindeki yetkisidir, source:"م ل ك,B003"}.

<!-- v16:augment brief=augment9 model=opus para=2 kind=refs -->
Ayrıca: {source:59:23} {source:62:1} "el-melik" adının Allah için kullanılması; {source:54:55} "melîk" kelimesinin Kur'an'da Allah için geçmesi

Gün art arda iki kez sorulur: {ar:وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ, tr:ve mâ edrâke mâ yevmü'd-dîn, gloss:din gününün ne olduğunu sana ne bildirdi, source:82:17}, {ar:ثُمَّ مَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ, tr:sümme mâ edrâke mâ yevmü'd-dîn, gloss:sonra, din gününün ne olduğunu sana ne bildirdi, source:82:18}. "Temlikü" ile "mâlik" aynı köktendir. Kur'an'ın kendi tarifinde din günü, sahip olmak fiilinin herkes için olumsuz söylendiği gündür. O gün bir sahip vardır, çünkü öteki bütün sahiplikler düşmüştür. Mülk her zaman O'nundur, ama dünyada insanlara da bir sahiplik verilir. Üç yüz kırk dokuzuncu değil, yukarıdaki dua bunu açıkça söyler: {ar:تُؤْتِى ٱلْمُلْكَ مَن تَشَآءُ وَتَنزِعُ ٱلْمُلْكَ مِمَّن تَشَآءُ, tr:tü'ti'l-mülke men teşâü ve tenzi'u'l-mülke mimmen teşâ, gloss:mülkü dilediğine verirsin, dilediğinden çekip alırsın, source:3:26}. Mülk verilen ve geri alınan bir şeydir. Başka bir yerde insanların ortaya çıktığı ve hiçbir şeylerinin Allah'tan gizli kalmadığı bir gün anlatılır. O gün bir soru sorulur ve cevabını soran kendisi verir: {ar:لِّمَنِ ٱلْمُلْكُ ٱلْيَوْمَ ۖ لِلَّهِ ٱلْوَٰحِدِ ٱلْقَهَّارِ, tr:li-meni'l-mülkü'l-yevm, lillâhi'l-vâhidi'l-kahhâr, gloss:bugün mülk kimindir? Bir ve her şeye galip gelen Allah'ın, source:40:16}. Mülkün kimde olduğu sorusunun dünyada birçok cevabı vardır. Din günü bu sorunun tek bir cevabının kaldığı gündür.

<!-- v16:augment brief=augment9 model=opus para=3 kind=refs -->
Ayrıca: {source:2:48} {source:2:123} hiçbir kimsenin başka bir kimse yerine bir şey ödeyemediği gün; {source:31:33} babanın çocuğu, çocuğun da babası yerine hiçbir şey ödeyemeyişi; {source:44:41} dostun dosta hiçbir fayda vermeyişi; {source:82:15} {source:82:16} sorudan hemen önce din gününün ateşe girilen gün olarak anılması; {source:77:14} aynı "mâ edrâke" sorusunun ayırma günü için sorulması; {source:6:73} {source:22:56} {source:45:27} o gün mülkün O'nun olması: sûra üfürüldüğünde, aralarında hüküm verirken, batıl ehli hüsrana uğrarken; {source:14:48} insanların bir ve kahhâr olan Allah'ın huzuruna çıkması; {source:2:107} {source:3:189} {source:5:120} {source:7:158} {source:9:116} {source:24:42} {source:25:2} {source:57:5} göklerin ve yerin mülkünün her zaman O'na ait olması; {source:25:3} {source:35:13} Allah'tan başka çağrılanların hiçbir şeye sahip olmaması; {source:72:21} peygamberin bile başkaları için ne zarara ne doğruya sahip olduğunu söylemesi

## Güneşle ölçülmeyen gün

"Gün" kelimesinin gündelik anlamı güneşe bağlıdır: {ar:اليوم مقداره من طلوع الشمس إلى غروبها, tr:el-yevmü mikdâruhû min tulû'i'ş-şemsi ilâ gurûbihâ, gloss:günün ölçüsü güneşin doğuşundan batışına kadardır, source:"ي و م,B001"}. Bir kelimenin akrabalarından gelen görüntüler, kelimenin bu ayetteki anlamının yerine geçmez, o anlamın yanında duyulur. Güneşin tepeye dikilip gölgenin kaybolduğu öğle anını altıncı ayetin {ar:ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ, tr:el-müstakîm, gloss:dosdoğru, source:1:6} kelimesi adlandırır. Bu ayetteki "yevm" o gökyüzü sahnesine güneşle ölçülen günü verir.

<!-- v16:augment brief=augment9 model=opus para=4 kind=refs -->
Ayrıca: {source:10:5} {source:17:12} güneşin ve gündüzün, yılların sayısı ve hesap bilinsin diye kılınması

Zümer suresinde sûra üfürülmesiyle başlayan sahne, kitabın konması, peygamberlerin ve tanıkların getirilmesi ve her kişiye yaptığının tam ödenmesiyle sürer. Sahne şu sözle kapanır: {ar:وَقُضِىَ بَيْنَهُم بِٱلْحَقِّ وَقِيلَ ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ, tr:ve kudıye beynehüm bi'l-hakkı ve kîle'l-hamdü lillâhi rabbi'l-âlemîn, gloss:aralarında hak ile hüküm verildi ve "hamd âlemlerin Rabbi Allah'adır" denildi, source:39:75}. Fâtiha'nın ikinci ayetindeki söz, aynı kelimelerle, hükmün verildiği günün son cümlesi olarak duyulur. Fiil edilgendir ve sözü kimin söylediği bildirilmez. Aynı ayette melekler Arş'ın çevresini kuşatmış, Rablerini hamd ile tesbih ederken görülür.

<!-- v16:augment brief=augment9 model=opus para=1 kind=refs -->
Ayrıca: {source:28:70} hamdin hem ilk hayatta hem âhirette O'na ait olması ve hükmün O'nun olması; {source:34:1} âhiretteki hamdin de O'na ait olması; {source:10:10} cennettekilerin son sözünün "el-hamdü lillâhi rabbi'l-âlemîn" olması; {source:83:6} insanların âlemlerin Rabbi için ayağa kalktığı gün; {source:3:27} {source:6:13} zamanın sahipliği: geceyi gündüze katması, gecede ve gündüzde barınan her şeyin O'nun olması

Kelimenin yazısında mim harfinin üstündeki küçük elif uzun "â" sesini gösterir. Harflerin gövdesi m-l-k'dir. Kur'an Allah'ı bu kökten iki ayrı kelimeyle anar. Peygambere şöyle dua etmesi söylenir: {ar:قُلِ ٱللَّهُمَّ مَٰلِكَ ٱلْمُلْكِ, tr:kulillâhümme mâlike'l-mülk, gloss:de ki: Allah'ım, ey mülkün sahibi, source:3:26}. Kur'an'ın son suresinde ise sığınılan, "insanların Rabbi"dir ve hemen ardından O, {ar:مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ, tr:meliki'n-nâs, gloss:insanların hükümdarı, source:114:2} ve {ar:إِلَٰهِ ٱلنَّاسِ, tr:ilâhi'n-nâs, gloss:insanların ilahı, source:114:3} diye anılır. Rab, hükümdar ve ilah sırası Fâtiha'daki Allah, Rab ve sahip sırasıyla aynı malzemeden kurulur. "Mâlik" (sahip) ile "melik" (hükümdar) aynı kökten iki ayrı kelimedir. Araplar ikisini Allah için yan yana da söylerdi: {ar:الملك لله المالك المليك, tr:el-mülkü lillâhi'l-mâliki'l-melîk, gloss:mülk, sahip ve hükümdar olan Allah'ındır, source:"م ل ك,B003"}. Sahip elinde tuttuğunu kullanır. Hükümdar ise bir topluluğu yönetir: {ar:الملك هو المتصرف بالأمر والنهي في الجمهور, tr:el-melikü hüve'l-mütesarrifü bi'l-emri ve'n-nehyi fi'l-cumhûr, gloss:melik, topluluk üzerinde emir ve yasakla tasarruf edendir, source:"م ل ك,B003"}. Türkçede "memleket" bugün insanın doğup büyüdüğü yer ya da bir ülke demektir. Arapçada ise kelime toprağı değil, bir yetkiyi adlandırır: {ar:المملكة سلطان الملك في رعيته, tr:el-memleketü sultânü'l-meliki fî raiyyetih, gloss:memleket, hükümdarın halkı üzerindeki yetkisidir, source:"م ل ك,B003"}.

<!-- v16:augment brief=augment9 model=opus para=2 kind=refs -->
Ayrıca: {source:59:23} {source:62:1} "el-melik" adının Allah için kullanılması; {source:54:55} "melîk" kelimesinin Kur'an'da Allah için geçmesi

Kur'an bu ayetin sorusunu bir yerde kendisi sorar ve cevabını bu ayetin ilk kelimesiyle verir. Gün art arda iki kez sorulur: {ar:وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ, tr:ve mâ edrâke mâ yevmü'd-dîn, gloss:din gününün ne olduğunu sana ne bildirdi, source:82:17}, {ar:ثُمَّ مَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ, tr:sümme mâ edrâke mâ yevmü'd-dîn, gloss:sonra, din gününün ne olduğunu sana ne bildirdi, source:82:18}. Cevap şudur: {ar:يَوْمَ لَا تَمْلِكُ نَفْسٌۭ لِّنَفْسٍۢ شَيْـًۭٔا ۖ وَٱلْأَمْرُ يَوْمَئِذٍۢ لِّلَّهِ, tr:yevme lâ temlikü nefsün li-nefsin şey'â, ve'l-emru yevmeizin lillâh, gloss:o gün hiçbir kimse bir başkası için hiçbir şeye sahip olamaz; o gün emir Allah'ındır, source:82:19}. "Temlikü" ile "mâlik" aynı köktendir. Kur'an'ın kendi tarifinde din günü, sahip olmak fiilinin herkes için olumsuz söylendiği gündür. O gün bir sahip vardır, çünkü öteki bütün sahiplikler düşmüştür. Mülk her zaman O'nundur, ama dünyada insanlara da bir sahiplik verilir. Üç yüz kırk dokuzuncu değil, yukarıdaki dua bunu açıkça söyler: {ar:تُؤْتِى ٱلْمُلْكَ مَن تَشَآءُ وَتَنزِعُ ٱلْمُلْكَ مِمَّن تَشَآءُ, tr:tü'ti'l-mülke men teşâü ve tenzi'u'l-mülke mimmen teşâ, gloss:mülkü dilediğine verirsin, dilediğinden çekip alırsın, source:3:26}. Mülk verilen ve geri alınan bir şeydir. Başka bir yerde insanların ortaya çıktığı ve hiçbir şeylerinin Allah'tan gizli kalmadığı bir gün anlatılır. O gün bir soru sorulur ve cevabını soran kendisi verir: {ar:لِّمَنِ ٱلْمُلْكُ ٱلْيَوْمَ ۖ لِلَّهِ ٱلْوَٰحِدِ ٱلْقَهَّارِ, tr:li-meni'l-mülkü'l-yevm, lillâhi'l-vâhidi'l-kahhâr, gloss:bugün mülk kimindir? Bir ve her şeye galip gelen Allah'ın, source:40:16}. Mülkün kimde olduğu sorusunun dünyada birçok cevabı vardır. Din günü bu sorunun tek bir cevabının kaldığı gündür.

<!-- v16:augment brief=augment9 model=opus para=3 kind=refs -->
Ayrıca: {source:2:48} {source:2:123} hiçbir kimsenin başka bir kimse yerine bir şey ödeyemediği gün; {source:31:33} babanın çocuğu, çocuğun da babası yerine hiçbir şey ödeyemeyişi; {source:44:41} dostun dosta hiçbir fayda vermeyişi; {source:82:15} {source:82:16} sorudan hemen önce din gününün ateşe girilen gün olarak anılması; {source:77:14} aynı "mâ edrâke" sorusunun ayırma günü için sorulması; {source:6:73} {source:22:56} {source:45:27} o gün mülkün O'nun olması: sûra üfürüldüğünde, aralarında hüküm verirken, batıl ehli hüsrana uğrarken; {source:14:48} insanların bir ve kahhâr olan Allah'ın huzuruna çıkması; {source:2:107} {source:3:189} {source:5:120} {source:7:158} {source:9:116} {source:24:42} {source:25:2} {source:57:5} göklerin ve yerin mülkünün her zaman O'na ait olması; {source:25:3} {source:35:13} Allah'tan başka çağrılanların hiçbir şeye sahip olmaması; {source:72:21} peygamberin bile başkaları için ne zarara ne doğruya sahip olduğunu söylemesi

## Güneşle ölçülmeyen gün

"Gün" kelimesinin gündelik anlamı güneşe bağlıdır: {ar:اليوم مقداره من طلوع الشمس إلى غروبها, tr:el-yevmü mikdâruhû min tulû'i'ş-şemsi ilâ gurûbihâ, gloss:günün ölçüsü güneşin doğuşundan batışına kadardır, source:"ي و م,B001"}. Bir kelimenin akrabalarından gelen görüntüler, kelimenin bu ayetteki anlamının yerine geçmez, o anlamın yanında duyulur. Güneşin tepeye dikilip gölgenin kaybolduğu öğle anını altıncı ayetin {ar:ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ, tr:el-müstakîm, gloss:dosdoğru, source:1:6} kelimesi adlandırır. Bu ayetteki "yevm" o gökyüzü sahnesine güneşle ölçülen günü verir.

<!-- v16:augment brief=augment9 model=opus para=4 kind=refs -->
Ayrıca: {source:10:5} {source:17:12} güneşin ve gündüzün, yılların sayısı ve hesap bilinsin diye kılınması

EOF`;

text(r.output || `appended (exit ${r.exit_code})`);

const cmd = `cat > '/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s001/discovery/pilot1-20261005/1_4/luna/followup.tsv' <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Dan.7.14	Aramaic malkû, dominion	Daniel’s Aramaic malkû names the enduring kingdom given to the humanlike figure; it is cognate with the commentary’s labeled Arabic m-l-k and appears in a scene where all peoples serve the ruler.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.34.6	Compassion before judgment	God names himself compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in covenant love; this is a close biblical pairing for the commentary’s Rahman/Rahim immediately before the title “owner of the Day.”
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.34.7	Forgiveness without erasing guilt	The same self-revelation says God forgives wrongdoing yet does not simply clear the guilty; this preserves both mercy and accountability in the sequence the commentary develops.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.24.12	Heart weighed and deeds repaid	The proverb asks whether the one who weighs hearts will not know, then says he repays each according to work; it joins hidden motives to exact recompense in one passage.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.96.13	The Lord comes to judge the world	The psalm says the Lord comes to judge earth and peoples with righteousness; creation’s response makes this a compact scene of universal judgment, not just a shared “day” word.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Zeph.1.15	Wrath, darkness, and trumpet alarm	The next verse after Zephaniah’s approaching day names distress, darkness, and a trumpet blast; it adds the day’s sensory and cosmic disturbance to the commentary’s non-solar event.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.103.11	Mercy exceeds deserved repayment	WLC numbering includes the psalm heading; this is English Psalm 103:10. The psalm says God has not treated people according to their sins, a concrete counterweight to the commentary’s full repayment and merciful creditor.
strong	tevrat	paralel	Testament of Abraham, Recension A 13	Deeds weighed in the afterlife	Abraham’s vision shows a soul assessed by its deeds on a balance; this is a Jewish apocalyptic counterpart to the commentary’s upright scale and final account.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	2 Maccabees 12:44-45	Prayer and offering for the dead	Judas arranges atonement for fallen soldiers in hope that they may be freed from sin; this gives a different account of aid across death from the commentary’s claim that no one can pay another’s due.
strong	tevrat	motif	Unetanneh Tokef, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur liturgy	Creatures pass before the King and records seal fate	The prayer pictures all creatures passing before God, with life and death written and sealed; it extends the commentary’s sovereign day, personal account, and written verdict in a Jewish liturgical setting.
strong	tevrat	paralel	1 Enoch 62:2-3	Kings face the enthroned judge	The kings and mighty see the Son of Man on the throne and are overcome with fear while the righteous stand before him; this adds the commentary’s royal sovereignty and the collapse of worldly rank to Enoch’s court scene.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.12.36	Every spoken word answered for	Jesus says people will give account on the day of judgment for careless words; this gives a concrete relation between the commentary’s loss of speech-rights and the court’s accounting.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.24.36	The day’s date is not disclosed	Jesus says no one knows the day or hour; alongside the commentary’s answer to “when?” by describing what happens rather than naming a date, it keeps the reader’s attention on the event and readiness.
strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:1Pet.4.5	Judge of living and dead	 Peter says all will give account to the one ready to judge the living and the dead; this gathers the commentary’s death scene, universal judgment, and personal accounting in a concise Christian formulation.
strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Rev.20.13	Death and Hades release their dead	The next verse after John’s opened books says sea, Death, and Hades give up the dead for judgment; it adds the gathering of every person from death’s custody to the commentary’s tribunal scene.
EOF`;
const r = await tools.exec_command({cmd, workdir: "/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation", max_output_tokens: 1000});
text(r.output || `wrote followup file (exit ${r.exit_code})`);
